title: Course-Specific AI Tutors
answer: Course-specific AI tutors are assistants built around the material, sequence and assessment style of one particular course rather than a general purpose chatbot. They answer questions using that course's readings, lecture notes, problem sets and past exams, and they are usually introduced by the instructor who teaches it. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Course-specific AI tutors are assistants built around the material, sequence and assessment style of one particular course rather than a general purpose chatbot. They answer questions using that course's readings, lecture notes, problem sets and past exams, and they are usually introduced by the instructor who teaches it. The scope covers question answering, worked examples, hints on assignments and revision support, and it stops at the boundary of the syllabus the instructor has chosen to expose.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most of these tutors run on a retrieval layer over the course documents plus a hosted language model, with the retrieved passages passed to the model as context. Some are built inside a learning management system, others as a separate web app or chat interface that students reach with a course login.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with collecting and cleaning the course corpus, then chunking it, embedding it and indexing it for retrieval. The instructor writes the system prompt and the guardrails, decides what the tutor may and may not answer, and tests it against real student questions before the term begins. After launch the usual loop is log review, spot checks on answers, and small edits to the corpus or prompt when the tutor drifts from the course's own conventions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main questions are who owns the course material fed into the tutor, what student interaction data is retained, and whether the tutor's answers count as instruction the institution stands behind. Instructors generally need permission to upload copyrighted readings, and students need to know what is logged and who can read it. Provenance matters too, so a good tutor cites the specific reading or slide it drew on, and this site's own practice of linking to the original paper rather than a search tool reflects the same principle.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter integration with grading and feedback systems, so a tutor can see a student's submitted work and respond to it directly. Evaluation is likely to move from anecdote to shared benchmarks built from real course questions, and institutions will keep pressing on data retention and disclosure. The open question is whether these tutors stay a supplement to the instructor or start to carry part of the teaching load, and that will be settled by departmental policy as much as by the technology.
